newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission to report most states ready for euro.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission to report most states ready for euro.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to report on Wednesday that the majority of the European Union's members have their 1997 budget deficits under control and most will be ready to join a single currency, EU officials said.

The twice-yearly review of EU economic and budgetary conditions, often criticised for being politically influenced, is expected to forecast that only Italy and Greece could be unable to wrestle public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- the Maastricht treaty target.

In a rare breach of protocol, EU Commissioner Emma Bonino on Monday lashed out at the forecasts, calling them "unbalanced" because of a widely leaked estimate putting Italy's 1997 deficit at 3.2 percent of GDP.
The Commission weathers heavy pressure when preparing the sensitive forecasts, which indicate members' progress in meeting Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) criteria.

The EU executive's report will also mark a clear difference of opinion from that of the more critical views of Europe's central bank-in-waiting -- the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the sources said.
Both institutions play a critical role in weighing the economic and budgetary health of EU governments ahead of the decision on EMU participation, due a year from now.
The economic convergence reports from the two bodies will aid EU finance ministers in deciding which countries should enter the single currency.
In its latest annual report, the EMI said most EU governments still had further work to do in curbing public expenditure, a view echoed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
A senior IMF official on Monday warned that Germany, France and Italy all needed to do more to cut their budget deficits in order to qualify for EMU.
The IMF offers its own forecasts for the EU's budgetary and economic performance later this week.
In addition to 1997 forecasts on deficits, debt, GDP growth and inflation, the Commission will also look ahead to 1998, providing markets with important food for thought.
EU policy-makers have repeatedly argued that budgetary consolidation efforts by governments must be judged in terms of sustainability and not just their performance in 1997.
For Italy, this is seen as a particular problem given the heavy burden of one-off savings measures contained in its latest 1997 budget blueprint.

And while Germany and France, the two main engines behind the drive towards monetary integration, are expected to win a favourable review from the EU, expectations in the private sector are for additional spending and tax measures.
France, now facing a snap election in a matter of weeks, is widely seen to be in need of a cash boost from social security charges this year.
Germany, struggling under the weight of record unemployment, may require a supplementary budget of 15 to 20 billion marks ($11.7 billion).

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday said Bonn would do everything necessary to meet the Maastricht deficit target but any further actions could only be determined in May after a review of tax estimates.
Analysts say currency markets tend to discount the Commission's forecasts unless they show something that obviously goes against what the Commission, a keen advocate of EMU, would want to report.
The EU executive denies that it seeks to throw a positive light on the forecasts, emphasising the professionalism and experience of its analysts. ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
